title: Rolling-State DP: When to Use It

writing.exampleCaption: Complete std-only rolling-dp program for its typed teaching fixture. Parsing and output construction are separate from the core algorithm.
writing.explanation:
For costs [10,15,20], costs to land on each stair are 10,15,30. Moving beyond the last stair costs min(15,30)=15. You may start at stair 0 or 1; the final answer is not necessarily the cost at the last stair.

The worked program is a complete executable for this pattern. Its core function uses typed input so the state transitions remain visible. The challenge input contract is: Return the minimum cost to move beyond the final stair. The visible fixture is `cost=[10,15,20]` and its example result is `15`. The implementation and additional semantic fixtures were checked against an independent reference calculation. Those bounded tests establish these examples; they are not a proof for all inputs or a measurement on an iPhone.

Return a canonical String from solve: lowercase true/false for booleans; decimal integers without extra signs, leading zeros or whitespace; comma-separated sequence values and semicolon-separated groups. Whole-number medians have no decimal suffix; half medians use .5. Do not append a newline to the returned value. Preserve the explicitly named textual sentinels such as none or #. Input fixtures are bounded so the demonstrated arithmetic fits its named Rust types; satisfy the stated input preconditions before applying the algorithm.

String and character-grid fixtures use ASCII unless the lesson explicitly specifies Unicode scalar values.

A problem is a good match for Rolling-State DP when it asks for constant-space Fibonacci-like recurrences. Here the concrete task is: Return the minimum cost to move beyond the final stair. The visible input `cost=[10,15,20]` is an example, not a definition of the whole problem. Ask what operations the solution must support and what the input guarantees. Choose a recurrence when subproblems overlap. `Some` patterns summarize a frontier instead of a full DP table; either representation needs an invariant, and any greedy shortcut needs proof. The right choice follows from those guarantees, not from a familiar noun in the prompt.

The decisive invariant is: Discard table entries once no future transition can read them. Try to say why it applies to the task without quoting the implementation. Which fact becomes known after one update, and which possible answers remain? A one-dimensional DP state summarizes a prefix or a single parameter. Define its meaning before writing a recurrence. If that claim cannot be maintained on a legal input, the pattern is wrong or one of its preconditions is missing. A counterexample is more useful than a vague warning: change one property of the sample, trace the first two steps, and identify the exact claim that fails.

Compare costs before committing. The advertised bound is O(n) time · O(1) space; identify the operation responsible for it and the extra memory it needs. Then compare a straightforward alternative: a direct scan, full sort, or repeated recomputation may be easier but can pay for the same work many times. Do not choose the more elaborate method just because it has a famous name. For the sample, predict `15` and explain which part of the state lets the method reach that result.

When the prompt is ambiguous, ask about input size, ordering, duplicates, and required output format. Test the base state, the first transition, impossible states, and whether an in-place update accidentally reuses an item twice. Use `Option` or a safe sentinel for unreachable states, and choose an iteration direction that matches the recurrence's dependencies. The Rust sketch can show a useful primitive without proving that the whole task is solved; connect each primitive to the requested output. You should be able to name a fitting case, a near miss, and the assumption separating them before writing the first line.
